title.analysis: Authentic title "Why Stable Jobs Are Financially Riskier Than Ever In 2026" is a contrarian "why X is riskier" reframe with a year stamp. The script delivers on it with a concentration-risk argument and a layoff burn-rate scenario. It performed TYPICAL against nearest-age peers that include the channel's large threshold hit "Why Everything Changes After Paying Off Your House" and "10 Unsexy Habits That Make Serious Money". Association only; no CTR or experiment evidence.

script.stored_text_completeness: All 20261 canonical characters read sequentially in full in 1 bounded ranges; auto-generated untimed text; stored ending is complete ("everyone else is still assuming they have."); ASR artifacts ("I company slack", "for for", "On standard advice"); 3,403 words over 1,404 seconds (~145 wpm) is consistent with a full read; audio, timed delivery and editing unverified.
script.opening_words: Walk into the first apartment on a Tuesday morning in March. The guy who lives here is 34. His name is Daniel. Makes $118,000 a year as a senior analyst at a consulting firm. Good salary, great benefits. The kind of job you describe at Christmas dinner and watch your relatives nod approvingly. His phone buzzes at 7:12 a.m. Email from HR subject line, "Important update regarding your position." His laptop is already locked. Badge access revoked. Health insurance terminated
script.ending_words: stable has been quietly hiding for for The job title on your LinkedIn isn't your financial foundation. It's your current highest paying client. Treat it like one. Stability is not something your employer provides. It's a structure you build yourself. The people who understood that earliest aren't the ones taking risks. They're the ones who finally read the fine print on the deal everyone else is still assuming they have.
script.analysis: Full 20261 canonical characters read. A contrarian essay: two-neighbor cold open (laid-off salaried Daniel vs diversified freelancer Priya), decline of pensions and tenure, layoffs during record profits, concentration risk, AI exposure, a Marcus layoff burn-rate scenario, lifestyle lock-in, healthcare and vesting "handcuffs", behavioral explanations, and a call to build one outside income stream. Verified: BLS median tenure 3.9 years (lowest since 2002); KFF 2025 family premium ~$27,000 with ~$6,850 worker share; Meta first dividend $0.50/quarter. Wrong or non-reproducing: Meta "$3.9 million per cut employee" (~$243K from the dividend); mortgage share labelled take-home is actually gross; month-three and month-five savings do not reconcile with the stated $2,930 burn; $885 side income "three weeks of runway"; UI $4,200/month exceeds most state maximums. Several corporate and AI-exposure figures match known reports but were not fetched. The stored ending is complete.

COBRA cost and self-introduction with subscribe ask.

Marcus layoff scenario months one to five.
Loss aversion, Organization Man and sunk cost.
Income security: three streams, freelancing data, $885 side income.
Reassurance, one-question action item and close.

topic.analysis: Job security reframed as income concentration risk: single-employer dependence for salary, health insurance and retirement match, contrasted with diversified income.
topic.audience_problem: Salaried professionals who feel safe but are exposed to sudden layoffs and benefit loss.
topic.time_sensitivity: Medium: tied to 2023-2026 layoff and AI news cycles.
topic.narrative_angle: Contrarian: the "safe" job is the risky one.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Test an original layoff-runway explainer built on one reconciled month-by-month table (state UI caps, COBRA from KFF premiums, vesting rules) and a self-check calculator, keeping corporate-payout math reproducible.
topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test
